points: OIDC replaces persistent GitHub credentials with an identity token issued for the workflow.
The recommended workflow pattern delegates token exchange to the cloud provider's official action.
Enable the workflow's OIDC token permission at the job or workflow level.
useCases: Keyless deployments — A deployment workflow needs access to AWS, Azure, GCP, or another OIDC-capable provider without storing static cloud keys.
Short-lived cloud access — A workflow must receive temporary authorization for cloud resources during a deployment run.

industries.problem: Auditors reject static cloud keys in CI, so deploy jobs assume a role with a token tied to repo and branch.
Many service repos deploy to separate cloud accounts, and OIDC trust avoids rotating dozens of stored access keys.

source.label: Configuring OpenID Connect in cloud providers

cards.title: Events and triggers
cards.definition: GitHub Actions workflows start when configured events occur, such as pushes, pull requests, schedules, manual dispatches, or another workflow's run.
points: A trigger is the event declaration that causes GitHub Actions to create a workflow run.
Events can respond to repository activity, such as pushes and pull requests.
Use `schedule` with one or more cron expressions for recurring execution.
useCases: Continuous integration — Run validation for changes entering or landing in a repository.
Scheduled automation — Execute maintenance or reporting at recurring times.

industries.problem: Nightly cron-triggered jobs refresh product feed exports and run catalog checks without a developer starting them.
Pull request events start compliance linting on changes to patient-data code, so unreviewed edits can't merge unchecked.

cards.title: Deployment jobs
cards.definition: Deployment jobs sequence workflow work with `needs` and target a named environment with `environment`.
points: Use `needs` to make a later job wait for an earlier job, which lets a workflow express build-to-test-to-deploy sequencing.
Jobs are isolated execution units and receive their own runner or container rather than sharing one execution context automatically.
Attach one deployment target to a job through its `environment` property, such as `production`, `staging`, or `development`.
useCases: Sequential delivery stages — A pipeline should build first, test the result second, and deploy only after tests finish.
Gated production deployment — Production releases require human approval or branch restrictions.

industries.problem: Route-planning API releases must clear a staging deploy and health check before production, so dispatchers never get a broken build.
Claims-system deploys need a recorded history per environment, so auditors can see what reached staging versus production and when.

cards.title: Service containers
cards.definition: Run Docker-based databases, caches, web services, and other dependencies alongside a GitHub Actions job.
points: Service containers let a job run supporting databases, web services, caches, or similar dependencies alongside its steps.
Declare services separately for each job that needs them.
Each configured service gets a new Docker container and is removed after the job completes.
useCases: Test against PostgreSQL or another database — Integration tests need a real relational database.
Run a cache service — Application tests depend on an in-memory data store.

industries.problem: Shipment-tracking APIs need integration tests against a clean database each run, so no shared test server holds stale rows.
Cart and session code relies on Redis behavior, and a disposable cache container lets tests catch eviction bugs before release.

cards.title: Composite actions
cards.definition: Composite actions package multiple workflow steps behind one action.
points: A composite action groups a sequence of workflow steps behind one action interface.
The same grouped action can be invoked as one step from multiple workflows.
The action is described by an action.yml metadata file placed in its directory.
useCases: Share repeated commands — Several workflows need the same sequence of shell commands.
Organize a local action — A repository wants its automation helper kept with the workflows that use it.

industries.problem: Many network-service repos repeat the same license-header check and config linting steps, so one composite action keeps them identical.
Course-platform repos each repeat the same seed-database and lint steps, and one local composite action updates them all at once.

source.label: Creating a composite action - GitHub Docs

cards.title: Environments
cards.definition: Use a job-level environment to gate deployments with protection rules such as required reviewers.
points: Configure required reviewers on an environment to pause jobs that target it until an authorized person or team approves.
An environment secret is scoped to jobs that explicitly declare the corresponding environment.
Approval controls both deployment progression and when the job can access protected environment secrets.
useCases: Production approval gate — A production deployment should pause until an operations owner approves it.
Environment-scoped credential — A deployment needs a credential that must not be exposed to unrelated jobs.

industries.problem: Patient-portal releases wait for a compliance owner's approval before the job can read production database credentials.
Payment service deploys need sign-off from a release manager, so unreviewed workflows never touch live banking API secrets.

cards.title: Artifacts
cards.definition: Artifacts store files produced by a GitHub Actions workflow so they survive a job and can be shared with another job in the same run.
points: Artifacts package files generated by a workflow run so they can be transferred or retained.
Use artifacts both to preserve job output and to make it available to another job.
The producing job must assign a name and upload its files before it finishes.
useCases: Transfer build output — A compile job produces binaries that a packaging or deployment job needs.
Retain diagnostics — A workflow generates test reports, logs, or screenshots that developers must inspect after completion.

industries.problem: A build job on a macOS runner produces an IPA that a separate upload job needs, so it is passed along as a named artifact.
Firmware images and flash logs from CI builds must be kept for engineers to download and reproduce bench failures later.

cards.title: Matrix builds
cards.definition: Use a matrix strategy to run one job across combinations of versions, platforms, or other variables.
points: A matrix turns one reusable job definition into multiple generated job runs.
Declare each matrix dimension as a variable whose value is an array.
With several dimensions, GitHub runs the job for every Cartesian-product combination.
useCases: Version compatibility testing — Run tests against several language or runtime versions.
Cross-platform validation — Execute the same checks on Linux, Windows, and macOS runners.

industries.problem: A published SDK must work on every supported runtime and OS, and a matrix covers each combination without copy-pasted jobs.
A numerical library must give consistent results across Python and NumPy versions, so a matrix exposes version-specific numeric differences.

source.label: Running variations of jobs in a workflow

cards.title: Jobs and steps
cards.definition: GitHub Actions workflows divide work into jobs, and each job contains ordered steps.
points: A workflow can contain multiple jobs, and independent jobs start concurrently unless dependencies are declared.
Set needs on a job to make it wait for the jobs it depends on.
Every job must select its execution environment with runs-on.
useCases: Parallel validation — Run linting and tests concurrently to shorten feedback time.
Dependency-gated deployment — Require tests to pass before publishing or deploying.

industries.problem: Asset validation and engine unit tests run as independent jobs so artists get faster feedback on a commit.
A compliance-check job must finish before a packaging job starts, using needs to enforce that order for audits.

cards.title: Runners
cards.definition: Use `jobs.<job_id>.runs-on` to choose the machine that executes a job.
points: Set `jobs.<job_id>.runs-on` to select the machine type for a job.
A job may use a GitHub-hosted runner, larger runner, or self-hosted runner.
Choose a self-hosted machine by assigning its labels to `runs-on`.
useCases: Hosted continuous integration — Run ordinary CI on a maintained Linux image without managing machines.
Specialized self-hosted execution — Schedule work requiring custom hardware or software installed on an internal network.

industries.problem: Firmware tests need a board attached over USB, so labeled self-hosted runners wired to test rigs run the flashing jobs.
Training-regression checks need GPUs that hosted images lack, so runs-on labels send those jobs to GPU-equipped machines.

source.label: Choosing the runner for a job

cards.title: Read and write ratios
cards.definition: Classify a workload by its read/write mix before choosing a multi-Region architecture.
points: Start by classifying the workload as read-intensive or write-intensive; this classification is the framing decision for the architecture.
The dominant access pattern is not merely descriptive: it guides the choice of multi-Region topology.
When reads substantially outnumber writes, a read-local/write-global strategy is a candidate.
useCases: Read-local, write-global — Reads greatly outnumber writes and stale reads are acceptable.
Simpler active-active reads — Static or read-only content is served from multiple Regions.

industries.problem: Product pages get far more reads than price edits, so the read/write mix decides whether to replicate reads across Regions.
Machines stream telemetry nonstop while few users query it, so write-heavy traffic shapes where ingestion runs in each Region.

cards.title: Denormalization
cards.definition: Denormalization intentionally duplicates data across tables to reduce joins and simplify frequently used access paths.
points: Denormalization deliberately adds redundancy to the data model.
The duplicated information can be placed across multiple tables to serve reads directly.
Frequently read fields are the strongest candidates for duplication.
useCases: Reduce join work — A read path repeatedly joins related tables and its latency is material.
Optimize hot fields — A frequently requested field can be copied into the table serving the read.

industries.problem: Order and cart pages join orders, items and products on every view, so copying product names and prices onto line items speeds them up.
Timelines show author names and avatars for many posts at once, and storing them on posts avoids a user-table lookup per row.

cards.title: High-level diagram
cards.definition: A high-level system diagram gives a broad view of a workload or major subsection.
points: Use this diagram to communicate the overall shape of a complete workload or one significant subsection.
Show the major components, how they relate, and the broad path data takes between them.
Make interactions and dependencies directional with arrows.
useCases: Communicate the overall architecture before specifying individual components. — Early design review
Break a workload into major components and show how they connect. — Workload decomposition

industries.problem: Clinicians, integrators, and compliance staff need one shared picture of how lab results flow from instruments to patient records.
Product, backend, and ops teams need a common view of how catalog, cart, checkout, and fulfillment connect before splitting work.

cards.title: Circuit breakers and bulkheads
cards.definition: Circuit breakers stop calls to a dependency after failures indicate that continuing is pointless; bulkheads cap outstanding work so overload in one dependency does not exhaust shared resources.
points: Configure a failure threshold that opens the circuit and blocks subsequent traffic to the affected service.
Use a recovery interval and a probe call to test whether the dependency is healthy again.
A successful probe restores normal traffic by closing the circuit.
useCases: Fail fast during dependency failure — A remote service is timing out repeatedly and more attempts would amplify the incident.
Isolate dependency capacity — One downstream integration is consuming too many client threads or connections.

industries.problem: A slow credit-score provider must not tie up shared threads that balance and transfer endpoints need to stay responsive.
When the restaurant-menu sync service fails, the app stops calling it and serves cached menus instead of piling up hung requests.

cards.title: Partitioning and sharding
cards.definition: Partitioning divides data into separate stores; horizontal partitioning, or sharding, gives each store the same schema and a subset of rows.
points: Horizontal partitioning keeps the schema consistent across shards while assigning each shard a distinct subset of the data.
Separating data lets independent partitions be managed and accessed separately, reducing competition for shared resources.
Adding storage nodes can increase scale-out capacity instead of relying only on a larger single machine.
useCases: Scale beyond one store — A dataset or workload exceeds the practical capacity of one database instance.
Reduce contention — Independent partitions need separate capacity or operational management.

industries.problem: Trip and location records grow past one database, so sharding by city or region keeps writes and lookups spread across nodes.
Transaction history for millions of accounts overwhelms one ledger store, so sharding by account ID spreads load and keeps each account's rows together.

cards.title: Identifying bottlenecks
cards.definition: Find the resource or boundary that saturates first under representative load, then act on that dimension.
points: Track resource consumption continuously and reject or delay excess work once the selected boundary crosses its limit.
A bottleneck response can be scoped to particular users or tenants, preventing a single principal from consuming the whole shared resource.
Define explicit enforcement points such as a gateway, service, partition, or downstream dependency so the response is predictable.
useCases: Protect an API during bursts — A shared API receives sudden traffic spikes and must keep latency within its SLO.
Contain noisy neighbors — One tenant consumes disproportionate capacity in a multi-tenant service.

industries.problem: Playback start times degrade at evening peak, and finding whether origin bandwidth or manifest service saturates first targets the fix.
Settlement runs miss their window, and locating the saturated ledger partition or bank API quota avoids scaling the wrong tier.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.definition: Failure-mode analysis enumerates failures in critical workload flows, identifies affected dependencies and blast radius, and plans mitigations.
points: Start with critical flows, enumerate their components and dependencies, and identify where failures can occur.
Estimate which components and user-facing flows each failure can affect; this reveals the failure's blast radius.
Record both internal and external dependencies alongside flow documentation so hidden single points of failure become visible.
useCases: Expose single points of failure — Evaluating a new architecture before implementation
Map blast radius — Planning resilience for a critical user journey

industries.problem: A funds-transfer flow silently relies on one external identity provider, so its outage blocks logins and transfers until mapped.
Video visit booking depends on scheduling, notifications and a video vendor, and failure mapping shows which outage strands patients mid-appointment.

source.label: Architecture strategies for performing failure mode analysis

cards.title: Observability
cards.definition: Observability combines logs, metrics, and traces from applications, services, and containers.
points: Instrument workloads and infrastructure to emit logs, metrics, and traces as the foundation of observability.
Place collectors between producers and storage when telemetry needs normalization or added context.
Route telemetry to separate stores when each signal requires a specialized backend.
useCases: Cross-service monitoring — A distributed application needs a unified operational view.
Signal enrichment — Telemetry must be prepared before analysis.

industries.problem: Transfer failures span several services, and correlated logs and traces show which hop failed without guessing.
Playback stalls get traced to a specific CDN, encoder or container version by comparing metrics and traces across regions.

source.label: Observability with Logs, Traces, and Metrics - Observability ...

cards.title: Vertical and horizontal scaling
cards.definition: Vertical scaling replaces existing components with higher-capacity ones; horizontal scaling adds replica nodes to distribute work.
points: Start with the workload's performance requirements and measured bottleneck; there is no universally correct scaling direction.
An architecture may need horizontal scaling, vertical scaling, or a combination as demand rises.
Capacity planning includes scale-down behavior, not only adding resources during peaks.
useCases: Increase per-component capacity — A component is constrained by its available memory, storage, or processing capacity.
Add replica capacity — Demand exceeds the aggregate capacity of the current deployment.

industries.problem: Match servers fill up during evening peaks and sit idle at night, so fleets must grow and shrink with player counts.
A core ledger database on one primary hits memory limits at month-end, so teams weigh a bigger host against re-architecting.

cards.title: Consensus
cards.definition: Consensus lets distributed participants agree despite failures.
points: A mutex-based design grants leadership to the first participant that obtains the exclusive lock.
Followers need a liveness signal, commonly a heartbeat or polling, to detect that the current coordinator is no longer available.
Bully, Raft, and Chang–Roberts are examples of established leader-election algorithms.
useCases: Work coordination — A distributed worker pool needs exactly one instance assigning jobs.
Failover management — Replicated services must designate an active coordinator after failure.

industries.problem: Replicas must agree on one writable primary after a node crash so two nodes never accept conflicting writes.
Several dispatch service instances must agree on one owner of route assignments so no delivery is assigned to two drivers.

source.label: Leader Election pattern - Azure Architecture Center

cards.title: Relational versus non-relational
cards.definition: Choose relational databases for structured, strongly consistent transactional workloads and rich relationships.
points: Relational databases are a strong fit for transactional workloads that require ACID guarantees.
Choose a non-relational store when predictable, low-latency access patterns are more important than relational querying.
Relational databases use an explicit schema covering tables, columns, indexes, and relationships.
useCases: Strongly consistent transactions — Order checkout, inventory updates, or financial transactions requiring atomic multi-step changes.
Low-latency key access — User profiles, sessions, or other records retrieved directly by a stable key.

industries.problem: Usage charges, plans, and invoices must reconcile exactly, and constraints stop orphaned or duplicate billing records.
Player inventories and match state are fetched by player ID in milliseconds, so a key-based store fits better than join-heavy queries.

source.label: What is a NoSQL Database? - AWS

cards.title: Rate limiting and backpressure
cards.definition: Rate limiting deliberately restricts request throughput so a service stays within its capacity and avoids overload.
points: Per-client limits protect shared capacity from one noisy caller.
Rate limiting absorbs unpredictable traffic spikes by restricting the admitted request rate.
Expose an explicit retry signal so callers can reduce pressure and schedule a later attempt.
useCases: Overload protection — Protecting an API from sudden demand spikes
Fair resource allocation — Sharing limited capacity among tenants or clients

industries.problem: A merchant's retry storm after an outage can starve other merchants of authorization capacity unless each is limited.
On-sale moments flood seat-reservation endpoints, so admitting only a fixed rate keeps the inventory database from collapsing.

source.label: Rate Limiting Pattern - Azure Architecture Center

cards.title: Keyspace notifications
cards.definition: Keyspace notifications let Redis clients receive Pub/Sub events for key changes such as expiration and eviction.
points: They provide push-based observation of data-set changes, avoiding polling for keys that disappeared.
Expiry events can be scoped to a database, such as database 0.
Redis offers two notification families for each qualifying operation: keyspace and keyevent.
useCases: React to cache disappearance — A cache-maintenance worker removes related entries when a cached key expires or is evicted.
Track data-set activity — An observability consumer counts operations such as expirations or deletions by subscribing to an event pattern.

industries.problem: Held seats must return to sale the instant a checkout timer lapses, without polling thousands of hold keys.
Driver offer keys expire if unanswered, and dispatch must reassign the request immediately without scanning pending offers.

cards.title: Hot keys and large values
cards.definition: Find hot keys and oversized keys before scaling Redis.
points: A key cannot spread its workload across shards automatically; all of its requests target the shard that owns it.
A hot key can degrade latency for unrelated requests handled by the same overloaded shard.
Treat values or collections at roughly hundreds of kilobytes and above as candidates for large-key investigation.
useCases: Add an application-local cache for hot reads — Read-heavy traffic repeatedly targets one key.
Split an oversized value into smaller keys — One collection or payload consumes substantial memory and bandwidth.

industries.problem: One featured product or sale banner key takes most reads, saturating its shard and slowing unrelated cart lookups.
A celebrity's follower list stored as one huge set blocks the shard when read, delaying other users' timeline requests.

source.label: Redis Enterprise Software observability and monitoring guidance

cards.title: TTL and expiration
cards.definition: Set a TTL to remove cache keys automatically when their freshness window ends.
points: Use expiration to bound how long cached data remains available; the timeout is commonly called a TTL.
After the TTL elapses, Redis automatically removes the key.
EXPIRE assigns a relative lifetime to an existing key.
useCases: Freshness-bound response caching — Cache database or API responses for a defined freshness window.
Temporary state — Remove session, token, or temporary state after inactivity or a fixed lifetime.

industries.problem: Cached shipping quotes and promo prices go stale quickly, and a short TTL stops outdated prices being shown at checkout.
Login challenges and one-time passcodes must stop being valid after minutes, and TTL removes them without a sweeper.

cards.title: Replication and failover
cards.definition: Redis replication is asynchronous, so replica lag can leave recently acknowledged writes vulnerable during failover.
points: The primary normally sends the client acknowledgement without waiting for replica processing.
WAIT counts acknowledgements from the configured number of other Redis instances for preceding writes.
Replica lag is tracked through periodic pings and acknowledgements of the processed replication stream.
useCases: Require replica acknowledgements — A write should be copied to several replicas before the client proceeds.
Gate writes on replica health — A primary should stop accepting writes when too few healthy, current replicas exist.

industries.problem: A payment-intent write acknowledged by the primary can vanish on failover, causing duplicate charges or lost confirmations.
Match results and inventory grants held in Redis can roll back after a primary crash if the promoted replica was behind.

cards.title: RDB and AOF persistence
cards.definition: RDB periodically saves compact point-in-time snapshots, while AOF records write operations for replay during recovery.
points: RDB stores a compact, single-file image of the dataset at a particular moment, which is convenient for backup handling.
For large datasets, RDB can reduce restart time compared with reconstructing state from an AOF log.
AOF appends operations instead of updating earlier log positions, avoiding seek-based writes and the documented power-outage corruption concern.
useCases: Backup with RDB snapshots — Create compact backups or restore a dataset version from a known point in time.
Durable write logging — Reduce the amount of recent data exposed to loss after a restart by selecting an AOF synchronization policy.

industries.problem: Shopping cart and inventory counters in Redis must survive node restarts without losing recent orders or needing a full rebuild.
Player session and match state in Redis needs quick reloads after maintenance, with snapshots kept for rolling back to an earlier state.

cards.title: Cache stampede
cards.definition: A cache stampede occurs when a popular key expires and many requests regenerate it concurrently.
points: The failure pattern is synchronized expiration followed by duplicate backend regeneration for the same popular key.
Request coalescing turns concurrent misses into one backend fetch and waiting readers.
TTL jitter spreads expiration events and lowers the chance of a broad synchronized miss.
useCases: Single-flight regeneration — A high-traffic product or profile key expires and many requests arrive together.
Staggered expirations — Many related keys have similar lifetimes and tend to expire together.

industries.problem: A flash-sale product page key expires and thousands of shoppers trigger the same expensive inventory and pricing query at once.
A cached front-page article list expires during a traffic spike and every reader request re-runs the same CMS database query.

source.label: Cache Layer Architecture: A Practical Guide to Speed & Scale

cards.title: Lists
cards.definition: Redis Lists are insertion-ordered sequences of strings that support efficient operations at both ends.
points: A List stores string values in an ordered linked-list structure.
LPUSH adds one or more values to the left side of a list.
LPUSH can create the list key as part of adding the first value.
useCases: Task queues — FIFO work processing
Undo stacks — LIFO state reversal

industries.problem: Dashboards need the latest readings per device without a table scan, so new values are pushed onto a per-device list head.
Agents need a ticket's newest events shown first, so each update is prepended to that ticket's list in arrival order.

cards.title: Write-behind tradeoffs
cards.definition: Write-behind stores updates in Redis first and persists them to the backing database asynchronously.
points: The application’s first write targets Redis rather than the backing database.
A cache-side background process later persists the buffered change.
Write-behind can make requests faster and combine multiple updates before database persistence.
useCases: Write-heavy workloads — High-volume updates where lower request latency matters more than immediate database persistence.
Batch-friendly changes — Multiple updates can be combined before persistence to reduce backend write overhead.

industries.problem: Frequent player stat updates would overload the primary database if every change had to be persisted before the game responds.
Impression and click counts arrive in bursts, so persisting merged totals avoids one database write per event.

source.label: The complete guide to cache optimization strategies for developers

cards.title: Memory limits and eviction
cards.definition: Redis uses maxmemory to cap cache data and maxmemory-policy to decide what happens at the limit.
points: Set maxmemory to define the memory budget for cached data.
Choose maxmemory-policy according to whether the workload favors recency, frequency, randomness, expiration, or rejecting new writes.
Once usage passes the limit, Redis repeatedly removes policy-selected keys until memory falls below the configured threshold.
useCases: General-purpose LRU cache — A cache should retain recently accessed entries regardless of whether they have TTLs.
Write-rejection behavior — A cache must preserve all existing keys and surface memory pressure to the application.

industries.problem: Catalog and thumbnail caches grow with every new title, so old, rarely watched entries must be evicted to keep memory bounded.
Shipment-event buffers cannot silently lose entries, so writes must be rejected at the memory limit and the pipeline slowed.

cards.title: Streams
cards.definition: Redis Streams are append-only logs of field/value entries with ordered IDs.
points: Streams are append-only: entries are added to a log and are not edited in place.
Within one consumer group, Redis distributes messages across consumers so the group can process work in parallel.
A group maintains a delivery position representing the earliest entry it has not yet consumed.
useCases: Parallel worker processing — Multiple workers need to divide event processing while retaining acknowledgement state.
Independent event consumers — Several independent applications need to consume the same ordered event history.

industries.problem: Package scan events from many depots must be processed in order per shipment, and none may be lost when a tracking worker crashes.
Thousands of sensors emit readings in bursts, and a replayable log lets analytics workers catch up after downtime without dropping data.

cards.title: Sorted sets
cards.definition: Sorted sets associate unique string members with scores and keep them ordered.
points: Each member appears at most once and is positioned using its associated score.
ZADD supports both insertion and score changes in one command.
The first ZADD against a new key initializes the sorted set automatically.
useCases: Leaderboards — Maintain players ordered by points and retrieve the top or bottom ranks.
Scheduling — Store events or jobs with timestamps as scores and select items within a time window.

industries.problem: Home pages need a continuously updated ranking of most-watched titles without re-sorting view counts on every request.
Dispatchers must pull the next delivery stops ordered by deadline and re-prioritize them as promised times change.

cards.title: Cache invalidation
cards.definition: Invalidate cache-aside entries after updating the primary store, then let the next read repopulate them.
points: Perform the primary write before deleting the related cache key, so subsequent reads can rebuild the entry from current data.
After deletion, the first cache miss retrieves the authoritative value and can repopulate Redis.
Use GET and SET with an entry-specific expiration to constrain how long stale data can remain available.
useCases: Entity update invalidation — A user, product, or order record changes and its cached representation must no longer be served.
Cache-aside repopulation — A read-through cache should recover automatically after an explicit deletion.

industries.problem: A rescheduled or cancelled appointment must vanish from cached clinic availability so patients are not offered slots that are gone.
Cached shipment status must be dropped when a scan event updates the database, so customers stop seeing an outdated delivery stage.

cards.title: Connection lifecycle events
cards.definition: node-redis emits connect, ready, reconnecting, and end as connection lifecycle events.
points: node-redis exposes connection lifecycle events directly on the client object.
connect marks the beginning of a connection attempt and supplies no event argument.
ready is the event a pool can use to mark a client usable for Redis commands.
useCases: Pool health state — A connection pool needs to expose whether a client can currently execute Redis commands.
Connection telemetry — An application needs operational visibility into connection attempts and retry cycles.

industries.problem: Order-dispatch workers must know when their Redis client is usable again after a drop so they stop accepting orders until it is.
Network operations teams need reconnect and end events from session-store clients to alert on flapping links before subscribers lose service.

cards.title: Hashes
cards.definition: Redis hashes group an entity's named fields under one key.
points: A hash models one record as named fields grouped under a single Redis key.
Hashes suit lightweight objects and sets of related counters.
HSET both adds new fields and overwrites values for fields that already exist.
useCases: Basic objects — Store profile, configuration, or device attributes as separate named values.
Grouped counters — Keep related integer metrics under one entity key and update them independently.

industries.problem: Each device's settings and status must be read or patched field by field without rewriting a whole serialized JSON blob.
Views, shares and comments per article need independent increments under one key, avoiding a separate key for every metric.

cards.title: Rate limiting
cards.definition: Redis supports fixed-window, sliding-window, and token-bucket rate limiters.
points: Redis can support the three common policies—fixed window, sliding window, and token bucket—within one deployment.
A fixed-window counter uses INCR for the request count and EXPIRE to remove the completed window automatically.
Choose the Redis structure according to the algorithm: strings for counters, sorted sets for timestamp logs, and hashes for bucket fields.
useCases: Fixed-window API quotas — A simple quota per API key or route needs low memory and automatic cleanup.
Sliding-window protection — A high-value endpoint needs accurate recent-request tracking.

industries.problem: Tenants on different plans must stay within request quotas so one noisy customer cannot degrade shared endpoints.
Login and transfer endpoints need exact recent-attempt limits to slow credential stuffing without blocking legitimate users.

cards.title: Sets
cards.definition: Redis sets represent unordered collections of unique string members.
points: Sets enforce uniqueness automatically, making them useful for representing membership without maintaining a separate duplicate-checking structure.
A set can record distinct values such as visitors, tags, or feature flags associated with an entity.
Use a separate set key for a relation, such as the users assigned to a role.
useCases: Unique-item tracking — Track distinct visitors or identifiers associated with an object.
Relationship modeling — Associate users with roles, groups, or permissions.

industries.problem: Clinic staff portals must check quickly whether a user belongs to a care-team role before showing patient records.
Editors need distinct reader counts per article, but repeat visits and page refreshes inflate raw view totals.

cards.title: Reconnect strategy
cards.definition: Configure node-redis reconnection with a fixed delay, disablement, or a custom function.
points: Automatic reconnection is available after the client loses its server connection.
Configure reconnection behavior inside the client's socket options.
A numeric strategy creates a constant delay, expressed in milliseconds.
useCases: Recover from transient disconnects — A Redis instance is restarting or temporarily unreachable.
Spread fleet-wide retries — Many application instances share one Redis service.

industries.problem: Order-status caches briefly lose Redis during maintenance, and clients must resume on their own so tracking pages keep updating.
Appointment reminder workers must reconnect to Redis after network blips without manual restarts that delay patient notifications.

cards.title: Sentinel
cards.definition: Redis Sentinel monitors a Redis primary and its replicas, provides notifications and client discovery, and coordinates automatic failover.
points: Use Sentinel to add high availability to a primary-replica deployment that does not use Redis Cluster.
Continuous health checks let Sentinel detect problems with both the primary and replicas.
Applications and operators can receive notifications about monitored-instance problems.
useCases: Primary-replica high availability — Run a primary with replicas and need automatic recovery without adopting Redis Cluster.
Failover-aware service discovery — Let clients discover the current primary after topology changes.

industries.problem: Subscriber session and balance caches on a single primary need automatic promotion when it dies, with no manual intervention overnight.
Order-status and courier-location Redis must keep working through a primary crash during dinner peak, with apps finding the new primary.

source.label: High availability with Redis Sentinel | Docs

cards.title: Server-side scripts as hooks
cards.definition: Run Lua scripts or Redis Functions on the server to make multi-step reads and writes atomic.
points: Lua scripts move application logic into Redis, reducing client-server round trips for multi-step operations.
The entire script is indivisible from other clients' perspective.
A client observes the script before it has taken effect or after its complete effect, not a partial state.
useCases: Atomic conditional updates — A counter, quota, or token-bucket update must inspect current state before writing a new value.
Cross-key consistency — One logical operation must update related values stored under multiple keys.

industries.problem: Two buyers clicking the same seat at once must not both get a hold, so check and claim run as one script.
A wallet transfer must verify balance and debit one key and credit another, never exposing a half-applied state.

cards.title: Client error events
cards.definition: Node-Redis emits client errors through the `error` event.
points: The client exposes several lifecycle events, but `error` is the critical one for preventing unhandled client failures.
An `error` event is emitted whenever an error occurs inside the Redis client.
Every client should have an error listener as part of its initialization.
useCases: Protect initialization and connection setup — Application startup
Monitor transport and socket failures — Long-running service

industries.problem: A rate-limit client failing on a Redis socket reset must not crash the payment API with an unhandled error, dropping in-flight requests.
Session-presence services must log Redis client errors and stay up, so a network blip does not terminate the process and disconnect live rooms.

cards.title: Connections and pooling
cards.definition: Connection pooling reuses a bounded set of Redis connections, while multiplexing shares one connection across operations.
points: Redis client connection management has two principal models: pooling and multiplexing.
A pool starts with a small connection set instead of creating one socket for every request.
Borrowing marks a pooled connection as busy so concurrent operations can be coordinated.
useCases: Reuse connections across requests — Long-lived API service
Coordinate simultaneous Redis operations — Concurrent worker process

industries.problem: Search-result caches get hit by bursts of fare lookups, and unbounded Redis sockets would exhaust connection limits during peak sales.
Concurrent risk-scoring workers read many Redis keys per transaction, and sharing multiplexed connections keeps latency low without socket sprawl.

cards.title: Pub/Sub
cards.definition: Redis Pub/Sub broadcasts channel messages to currently subscribed clients in publication order.
points: Publishers name channels rather than individual recipients; subscribers independently register interest in those channels.
Within the documented Pub/Sub flow, consumers observe messages according to their publication order.
Each published message is delivered zero or one time; Pub/Sub provides no duplicate redelivery guarantee.
useCases: Cache invalidation signals — A cache entry changes and active application instances should promptly discard their local copy.
Transient fan-out events — Connected clients need ephemeral updates such as presence or live notifications.

industries.problem: Score and play updates must reach every connected viewer in order, and a missed tick is superseded by the next one.
Typing indicators and cursor moves must reach editors on every app server, though they're worthless seconds later.

cards.title: Client-side cache invalidation
cards.definition: CLIENT TRACKING enables server-assisted client-side caching.
points: CLIENT TRACKING turns on server-assisted client-side caching support for the connection.
Default tracking builds a per-connection record from keys read during the connection lifetime.
A modification to a tracked key triggers an invalidation notification.
useCases: Keep a local object cache coherent — A service keeps frequently read Redis objects in process memory and needs changes made by other clients to invalidate those entries.
Use same-connection invalidations — A RESP3 client wants invalidations alongside ordinary commands without maintaining a second message connection.

industries.problem: Every API request reads tenant plan limits, and local copies must refresh when billing changes a plan, without polling.
Per-order checks read instrument limits from Redis; local copies must refresh at once when risk teams change a limit.

cards.title: Stale-while-revalidate
cards.definition: Serve bounded stale data while refreshing when the product can tolerate temporary staleness.
points: Serve an acceptable cached value while refreshing asynchronously.
Track fresh and stale windows separately.
Stop serving stale data when its correctness window expires.
useCases: Product listing refresh — Serve a category page from a cached value just past its fresh window while one background job rebuilds it, then hard-expire it after ten minutes.
Exchange-rate snapshot — Show a cached currency rate for up to 30 seconds past freshness while a worker fetches the latest, but refuse anything older than the legal limit.

industries.problem: Forecast pages get heavy traffic, and slightly old data is fine but must be refreshed in the background without making readers wait.
Portfolio widgets can show slightly old quotes while refreshing, but must stop showing them once they pass the permitted age.

cards.title: Read-through caching
cards.definition: Place retrieval logic behind a cache abstraction so callers use one read contract.
points: Use a cache layer that loads missing values on behalf of callers.
Keep the loader's errors distinct from a valid missing record.
Coalesce concurrent loads for the same key.
useCases: Product detail loader — A catalog service calls one cache get for a SKU, and the cache runs the database query itself on a miss and stores the row.
Negative result handling — A user profile lookup stores a short-lived 'not found' marker, while a database timeout is raised to the caller and never cached.

industries.problem: Account-limit lookups must go through one read path, so a database timeout is never mistaken for an account with no limit.
Listing detail reads from many services should share one cache contract so none queries the property database directly with its own rules.

cards.title: Fan-out
cards.definition: Fan-out lets one event start many independently running Inngest functions.
points: A single event can start multiple independent functions without making their success or failure depend on one another.
Inngest matches the event name against registered triggers and starts every function that subscribes to it.
Every fan-out branch receives separate retry handling and observability.
useCases: Start separate signup workflows — A user signs up and needs onboarding actions.
Distribute work across owners — One business event must reach functions owned by different teams or applications.

industries.problem: A single order event must update stock, notify the buyer, and feed analytics without one failure blocking the others.
One lab-result event must update the patient record, alert the clinician, and sync billing, with each step retried independently.

source.label: Fan-Out Pattern | One Event, Many Functions - Inngest Docs

cards.title: Environments
cards.definition: Inngest environments separate production, shared non-production stages, and branch previews.
points: An environment is an operational boundary: its applications, functions, history, and credentials are maintained independently.
Use the production environment for live workloads rather than testing or preview deployments.
Choose a custom environment when several people or deployments need a shared staging, QA, or canary space.
useCases: Staging and QA — A team needs a shared pre-release space for integration testing and acceptance checks.
Branch preview validation — A deployment preview must test background functions without affecting production.

industries.problem: Order-confirmation and refund workflows can be tested end to end without sending real customer emails or charging cards.
Appointment reminder functions are verified in a separate stage so test events never reach real patients' phones.

source.label: Environments | Branch, Staging & Production - Inngest Docs

cards.title: Non-retriable errors
cards.definition: Use NonRetriableError to signal that another attempt cannot succeed, such as for invalid input.
points: Throw NonRetriableError to stop further retries for the function or step that encounters a permanent failure.
Choose it when repeating the operation cannot resolve the underlying problem.
Invalid input is a typical case because retrying does not change the bad input.
useCases: Reject invalid input — A request is missing a required field or contains invalid data.
Avoid repeated permanent failures — A known permanent condition would produce the same failure on every attempt.

industries.problem: Malformed patient-record events fail the same way each time, so retries only delay alerts to the team that must fix the source data.
Orders referencing discontinued or nonexistent SKUs cannot be fulfilled, so failing them at once frees workers and surfaces the error quickly.

cards.title: Observability
cards.definition: Use run traces to follow every operation in an Inngest execution and pinpoint slow or failed steps.
points: The trace combines execution timing, queue delay, retry history, and data inspection in one run view.
Use the waterfall timeline as the starting point for examining the run and choosing an individual operation.
The timeline distinguishes ordinary work from pauses, event waits, and calls to other functions.
useCases: Diagnose a failed run — A production run fails and the offending operation is unclear.
Find latency and queue delays — A workflow appears slow even though individual steps seem correct.

industries.problem: Support needs to see which step of a failed payout run broke and what data it received, without reading logs.
Order runs seem slow, and traces show whether the delay is queue wait, a slow carrier API call, or a planned pause.

cards.title: useRealtime
cards.definition: Subscribe a React component to an Inngest function's Realtime channel and selected topics with a server-issued token.
points: useRealtime connects a React component to messages emitted by an Inngest function.
channel identifies the Realtime stream; use a channel instance for automatic topic typing or pass a string.
topics limits the subscription to the channel topics the component needs.
useCases: Live job progress — Show progress or lifecycle state while a long-running Inngest function executes.
Streaming AI responses — Render streamed model output as tokens arrive and replace it with a final result.

industries.problem: Users stare at a blank page while large report exports run, so the UI shows live generation status instead.
Agents wait on AI-drafted replies with no feedback, so partial drafts appear in the ticket view as they are generated.

source.label: useRealtime() Hook | TypeScript SDK v4 Reference - Inngest Docs

cards.title: Batching
cards.definition: Batching groups matching events into one Inngest function run so a costly database or API operation can be performed in bulk.
points: The handler receives the whole group through events, allowing one bulk database or API operation.
The batching window starts with the first event that satisfies the function's trigger and optional filter.
Three independent finalization conditions can launch the run.
useCases: Bulk database writes — Many changes must be persisted efficiently.
Bulk API calls — A downstream API supports multi-item requests.

industries.problem: Millions of impression and click events would overload the warehouse if each triggered its own single-row insert.
Thousands of sensor readings arrive per minute and must be stored in grouped writes instead of one database call per reading.

cards.title: Event schemas
cards.definition: Event schemas define stable names and payload contracts so Inngest producers and consumers agree on event data.
points: Treat the event name and payload shape as a shared contract, allowing producers and consumers to change independently.
Put the event-specific payload in data; every triggered run receives that JSON object.
Reuse the declared event type in function triggers so the consumer is connected to the same typed contract.
useCases: Coordinate independent services — A billing service emits invoice-paid notifications consumed by downstream functions.
Share TypeScript event contracts — An application needs compile-time guarantees for custom event payloads.

industries.problem: Shipment-status events come from carriers and warehouses, and schemas keep tracking and alert functions from breaking on changed fields.
Claim-submitted events feed fraud, payout, and notice functions, and a shared payload contract keeps each team's changes from breaking the others.

cards.title: step.sleep and sleepUntil
cards.definition: step.sleep pauses an Inngest run for a relative duration, while step.sleepUntil pauses it until a chosen date and time.
points: Use step.sleep when the delay is relative to the point where the function reaches the step.
Use step.sleepUntil when execution should resume at a specific calendar moment.
The host does not need to keep a process alive during the pause.
useCases: Relative delay — A reminder should be sent a fixed interval after an event.
Calendar-time execution — A trial, deadline, or scheduled reminder has a known timestamp.

industries.problem: Trial-ending emails must go out at the exact trial expiry time without a worker idling for 14 days.
Filing deadline reminders must fire on set calendar dates, with no cron table or long-lived process to maintain.

cards.title: Automatic retries
cards.definition: Inngest automatically retries failed steps with backoff and jitter instead of immediately failing the function.
points: Retries are tracked independently for each step rather than shared across the function.
Automatic retries use a backoff schedule with jitter to avoid synchronized repeated requests.
Configure the number of retries with the function's retries option.
useCases: Recover transient infrastructure errors — Temporary network or database failures
Delay retries until an API-provided time — Rate-limited upstream APIs

industries.problem: A carrier label API times out mid-shipment, and automatic retries create the label without redoing earlier inventory steps.
Airline and hotel confirmation calls fail briefly during provider hiccups, and jittered retries avoid a retry stampede against the vendor.

source.label: Automatic Retries in Inngest | Config & Behavior

cards.title: Cancellation
cards.definition: Cancel an active Inngest function when a configured event arrives.
points: Each triggered run gets a cancellation listener waiting for the configured event.
Match cancellation data to the original trigger so one entity's event cannot cancel another entity's run.
A timeout can restrict how long the cancellation rule remains active.
useCases: Stop obsolete reminders — A user deletes a reminder while its delayed notification workflow is sleeping.
Cancel revoked work — A business object is revoked while its processing workflow is still active.

industries.problem: Customers who cancel mid-sequence keep getting trial-ending or payment-retry emails because the delayed workflow has no way to stop.
A traveler cancels a reservation while ticketing and itinerary-email runs wait, so matching by booking ID stops only that booking's work.

cards.title: onSendEvent
cards.definition: `onSendEvent` is an Inngest middleware lifecycle hook for outgoing events.
points: The lifecycle covers direct sends, step event sends, and step invocations.
`transformInput` is the place to enrich, normalize, or redact outgoing events.
Input transformation changes the event data centrally before transmission.
useCases: Central metadata enrichment — Add a consistent application, tenant, or source field to every outgoing event.
Central redaction — Remove credentials, tokens, or other sensitive properties before transmission.

industries.problem: Events from many services lack a tenant ID, so downstream functions can't scope work; middleware stamps it on every send.
Patient events can carry identifiers or notes by accident; redacting them centrally keeps PHI out of the event stream and its logs.

cards.title: Throttling and rate limiting
cards.definition: Throttle Inngest function starts to match a downstream API’s throughput limit.
points: Use throttling when work must be retained while matching a downstream service’s permitted throughput.
Queued runs are drained gradually and in FIFO order rather than being released as one burst.
Choose a period from one second to seven days, using one-second increments.
useCases: Match a vendor API quota — A downstream API accepts only a fixed number of requests per time window.
Absorb bursts without dropping work — Traffic arrives in bursts but every triggered job must be processed.

industries.problem: Campaign launches create thousands of send jobs at once, but the email provider caps sends per second and rejects any excess.
Nightly listing imports trigger thousands of geocoding calls, and a metered maps API throttles or bills for any overage.

cards.title: Priority
cards.definition: Prioritize urgent queued runs ahead of routine runs within the same function.
points: Priority chooses the next queued run inside one function rather than coordinating ordering across different functions.
Configure `priority.run` with a CEL expression that reads the triggering event.
The expression must produce an integer measured as a seconds-based priority factor.
useCases: Elevate urgent customer requests — A customer-facing request must be handled before routine queued work.
Prioritize by account plan — Different subscription tiers need different queue treatment.

industries.problem: Urgent escalation tickets wait behind bulk auto-replies in the same function, so priority lets them start first.
Enterprise tenants' report-generation runs get stuck behind free-tier jobs, so a plan-based priority runs them sooner.

cards.title: Timeouts
cards.definition: Bound a function run’s queue and execution time with `timeouts.start` and `timeouts.finish`.
points: Use `timeouts.start` to limit queue time before the run successfully starts its first step.
Use `timeouts.finish` to limit execution time after the function has started.
Configure both properties when the function needs separate bounds for startup delay and active execution.
useCases: Expire stale queued runs — Queued work loses value if it waits too long for capacity.
Enforce an execution deadline — A workflow must complete within a business or operational deadline.

industries.problem: Driver-match runs that sit queued past a rider's patience window are cancelled instead of dispatching a driver to a gone rider.
End-of-day reconciliation must finish before the settlement cutoff, so a stalled run is cancelled and escalated instead of hanging.

cards.title: Subscription tokens
cards.definition: Mint a scoped, short-lived subscription token on the server after authorizing the viewer.
points: Use getClientSubscriptionToken() in server-side code to create the browser-safe subscription credential.
The client receives both the token key and the environment-specific API base URL.
Authorization happens before token creation, so the token represents the server's access decision.
useCases: Resource-scoped realtime access — A user views live updates for one document, job, or thread.
Automatic token refresh — A React subscription may reconnect after the initial connection.

industries.problem: Team members must see live task updates only for boards they belong to, never other workspaces' boards.
Students watching a live grading or code-run result must not receive another student's submission stream.

cards.title: step.waitForEvent
cards.definition: Suspends a durable function run until a specified event matches or the timeout expires.
points: The run remains suspended until the specified event matches or the timeout ends.
The wait is durable and does not occupy an active function process.
The call accepts a stable ID and an options object containing event, timeout, and optional match settings.
useCases: Human approval — An invoice workflow waits for an approval event correlated by invoice ID.
Cross-function coordination — A function pauses until another function emits a completion event.

industries.problem: Account opening stalls until a customer finishes identity verification, and the run must resume on completion or flag the case if it lapses.
Held seats must be released if the buyer's payment confirmation never arrives, without a worker polling or idling during the hold window.

cards.title: Promise combinators
cards.definition: Promise combinators coordinate concurrent asynchronous operations.
points: The four standard combinators are all(), allSettled(), any(), and race().
all() requires universal fulfillment and fails at the first rejection.
allSettled() waits for every input to finish, whether it fulfills or rejects.
useCases: Require an aggregate success with all() — Several dependent requests must all succeed before rendering a page.
Audit every result with allSettled() — Independent jobs should all finish so successes and failures can be logged or summarized.

cards.title: Primitive values and coercion
cards.definition: JavaScript primitives are immutable values, while coercion converts values when an operation requires another type.
points: The main comparison choices are ==, ===, and Object.is(), each with different conversion and numeric edge-case rules.
Strict equality does not coerce operands before comparison.
Primitive coercion supplies a primitive when an operation requires one but does not strongly prefer String, Number, or BigInt.
useCases: Convert text explicitly before numeric calculations — Parsing user input
Use === when both type and value must match — Validation

cards.title: Iterables and generators
cards.definition: JavaScript iteration protocols let objects expose lazy synchronous or asynchronous sequences.

Generators support lazy pipelines: each requested value is calculated only when the consumer advances iteration.
useCases: Lazy sequence generation — Process large or unbounded sequences without storing every value.
Asynchronous data pipelines — Transform values from a stream or other asynchronous source as they arrive.

points: jest.resetModules() removes cached required modules so subsequent imports or requires receive fresh module instances.
Reset the registry when module-level state could make one test depend on another.
jest.isolateModules(fn) limits fresh loading to modules imported within its callback.
useCases: Fresh module state — A module stores mutable state at file scope and tests need independent instances.
Clean mock usage — Tests share spies or mocks whose call history must not affect later assertions.

cards.title: Spies and implementations
cards.definition: Observe an object method with jest.spyOn, or temporarily change its behavior with mockImplementation.
points: mockImplementation supplies the replacement behavior executed by the mock.
Replacing behavior does not remove call and instance tracking.
mockRestore returns the spied method to its pre-test implementation.
useCases: Observe interactions — Verify that code calls a real dependency method with expected arguments while retaining the method's normal behavior.
Override a dependency — Substitute deterministic behavior for a dependency during one test without permanently changing the object.

cards.title: Setup and teardown

points: Use beforeEach for repeated preparation and afterEach for repeated cleanup around each test.
Use beforeAll and afterAll when setup or teardown should happen once for a scope rather than once per test.
File-level lifecycle hooks cover every test in that file.
useCases: Isolate tests — Reset arrays, mocks, database fixtures, or other mutable data before each case and release per-test resources afterward.
Manage shared resources — Open a shared connection or create an expensive fixture once for a suite, then close it after the suite completes.

cards.definition: Jest mock functions replace behavior while recording calls, arguments, contexts, results, and constructed instances.
points: Call `jest.fn()` to create a standalone mock function for use in a test.
Mocks record each invocation and the arguments supplied to it, enabling interaction assertions.
When used as constructors, mocks retain the instances created through `new`.
useCases: Interaction testing — Verify that a collaborator was called with the expected arguments.
Controlled behavior — Return deterministic values for success, failure, or edge-case paths.

cards.definition: Snapshot testing records serialized output and compares later runs with that reference.
points: The workflow captures serialized output once and compares subsequent runs against the stored reference.
A mismatch fails the test and requires a judgment about whether the change is expected.
Snapshot verification happens on later executions rather than only when the reference is first created.
useCases: UI regression checks — Rendered UI or component output needs regression protection against unintended serialized changes.
Structured output verification — A stable object or structured value should be compared as a whole without writing many individual assertions.

The automatic mock is installed when the dependency is required.
A factory can customize the replacement, while options can alter mock behavior; both arguments are optional.

Select a user-module manual mock explicitly with jest.mock using the module path.

cards.title: Avoiding implementation details
cards.definition: Write tests around what users can find and do in the rendered UI, not component state, private methods, lifecycle methods, or child-component structure.
points: Model tests on real user workflows; similarity to actual use is the library’s confidence-building principle.
Keeping tests independent of internals helps implementation-only refactors avoid unnecessary failures.
Treat state as an implementation detail rather than a direct assertion target.
useCases: Refactor-resistant regression tests — A component’s internal state management changes while its visible behavior remains the same.
Accessible form workflows — A form must be tested from field discovery through submission feedback.

cards.title: Async UI

points: Use findBy when an element is expected to appear eventually: it combines single-element querying with asynchronous waiting.
A findBy call can receive query options first and waitFor options last, allowing its timeout and related waiting behavior to be customized.
Choose waitFor when the condition is an assertion or other callback result rather than simply finding one eventual element.
useCases: Await an eventual result — A loading indicator is replaced by a result after a request resolves.
Retry an assertion — A state change requires checking several DOM conditions.

points: It models the browser event sequence produced by a user action rather than sending only one chosen event.

cards.title: findBy and waitFor
cards.definition: Use findBy to await one element that should appear asynchronously; use waitFor to retry an assertion or custom condition until it succeeds or times out.
points: findBy combines immediate single-match querying with asynchronous retrying, making it the concise choice for an element that will appear later.
A findBy call can receive normal query options followed by waitFor configuration, allowing matching and timing concerns to remain separate.
Use findBy when the DOM update is delayed after an interaction and the test expects one matching element to appear.

Separate provider instances can give independently mounted feature instances isolated state.
Create the store lazily in component state so the instance remains stable across provider re-renders.

cards.title: Streaming responses
cards.definition: TanStack Start server functions can stream typed chunks using a ReadableStream or an async generator.
points: Streaming lets applications deliver server-produced data progressively, which is especially useful for incremental or AI-generated output.
Server functions can stream through either a Web ReadableStream or an async generator.
A handler may return a ReadableStream directly rather than assembling the complete result first.
useCases: Deliver partial output as it becomes available — AI and other incremental generation
Show progress or intermediate results before completion — Long-running server work

cards.title: Column ordering
cards.definition: Reorder displayed columns by supplying columnOrder as a sequence of column IDs, while leaving the column definitions unchanged.
points: Without explicit ordering state, the definitions array determines the visible sequence.
Set columnOrder when the UI needs a sequence different from the definitions.
Represent the desired sequence with column IDs rather than duplicating or rearranging definitions.
useCases: User-customized layouts — A data grid lets users choose which columns appear first without changing shared column definitions.
Context-specific ordering — Different screens use the same definitions but present fields in different business-priority sequences.

cards.title: Search middleware
cards.definition: Search middleware transforms query parameters before links are generated and after navigation validation.
points: Middleware changes the search object used to generate links belonging to a route and its descendants.
The same transformations are applied during navigation after validation, keeping generated URLs consistent.
Retention can be global with true or selective with an array of parameter names.
useCases: Retain shared context — A root-level filter or tenant key must remain available when navigating to descendant routes.
Strip default values — Pagination or sorting values should disappear from URLs when they equal schema defaults.

cards.title: Column and row pinning
cards.definition: Pin columns to the left or right while other columns remain in the center, and optionally split pinned regions into separate tables or use sticky CSS.
points: Column pinning is implemented through table state plus column and table APIs rather than a built-in visual layout.
Pinned columns may be rendered in separate start, center, and end tables, or kept in one table with sticky positioning.
Set initial pinned column IDs through columnPinning state or the initialState table option.
useCases: Persistent key columns — Keep identifier or action columns visible while horizontally scrolling a wide data grid.
Split-table layout — Render left, center, and right regions as separate tables for precise pinned-column layout.

cards.title: Async validators
cards.definition: TanStack Form supports async validators for server-backed checks such as username availability.
points: Use asynchronous validation when correctness depends on a server or another operation that does not complete immediately.
Choose an async trigger based on the user interaction that should initiate the remote check, such as change or blur.
Debouncing is configured directly on the form field instead of requiring a separate timing wrapper around the validator.
useCases: Availability checks — A username or email must be checked against records that already exist on the server.
Debounced remote validation — Typing should not issue a request for every keystroke.

industries.problem: Application forms run to a hundred conditional fields, and schema-driven validation keeps the rules in one place instead of duplicated in the browser and on the server.
Statutory forms must work without JavaScript and still validate identically, which progressive enhancement gives and a client-only form does not.

source.label: Form and Field Validation | TanStack Form React Docs

cards.title: Row selection
cards.definition: TanStack Table keys row-selection state by row ID.
points: Selection is stored against row IDs, making the identifier the link between selected state and the underlying record.
If no custom mapping is supplied, a row's position becomes its identifier.
For selectable data, choose an identifier that represents the record instead of its current position.
useCases: Preserve selection through reordering — A sortable or filterable table must preserve checked rows when visible ordering changes.
Keep selection stable across refreshes — Data is refreshed from an API and records may be inserted, removed, or paginated.
